title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
hookLine: Nathanael asks can anything good come from Nazareth

cards: Some towns come with a reputation. The one up the highway with nothing but a gas station. The neighborhood a family warns its kids about.
Then a friend runs up, breathless: we've found him, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, and he's from there. That's today's scene.
A man named Philip has just been called, and he goes straight to his friend Nathanael with the news. And Nathanael, hearing the name of the hometown, says out loud exactly what he thinks of it.

teach.h: CAN ANY GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, Nathanael answers: "Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" That's his whole review of the place. Philip doesn't argue.

He uses the words Jesus said to the first two disciples the day before: come and see. Nathanael comes, and as he walks up, Jesus says of him: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." No guile, no trickery.
It's almost a joke: the man who just insulted Jesus's town is praised for being honest.

teach.h: NO GUILE: HE SAID WHAT HE THOUGHT.
teach.b: He said exactly what he thought. Startled, Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him.

teach.h: I SAW YOU UNDER THE FIG TREE.
teach.b: And Jesus says: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. We aren't told what happened under the fig tree. Some readers imagine Nathanael was praying or studying there, but nobody knows.
What matters is that Nathanael knows, and it undoes him.

In one breath the skeptic says: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the King of Israel. Jesus answers: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.
An old tradition identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew. If that's right, the man who sneered at Nazareth became one of the twelve. The good thing came from the place he'd written off.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew on August 24, and on that day the Mass reads this Gospel of Nathanael under the fig tree, following the old tradition that they are the same man.

games.q: under the fig tree — tap the pairs.
p: can any good come from Nazareth?

s: the Gospel says what Nathanael was doing under the fig tree
it doesn't. the text is silent, and readers have only guessed.
Philip argued Nathanael out of his doubt
he didn't argue. he said: come and see.
the Church reads this Gospel on Saint Bartholomew's feast.

games.q: you're Philip. you've told your friend you've found the one the prophets wrote about, and he scoffs at the man's hometown. what do you do?
o: drop it and go back alone.
games.why: Philip just says come and see. Nathanael comes, is seen, and within a few lines calls Jesus the Son of God.

practice: Bring to mind a place you've written off, a town, a school, a kind of church, a corner of the internet, even a person's whole background, and notice if a little sneer comes with it, without scolding yourself.
Then picture one good person from there, real or imagined, walking toward you the way Nathanael walked toward Jesus. If you pray, ask to see that place more truly.

wordCard.voice: Fig tree. Where Jesus said he saw Nathanael before Philip even called him. The Gospel never says what happened there. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fig tree (John 1:48), where Jesus says he saw Nathanael.

carryVoice: Your line: can any good thing come. Philip's answer was three words: come and see. Until tomorrow.
